notes: Main-quest guide across The Naming (1), The Toll Hums (2) and Louder Than Books (3). The Naming's stages are named by id (quest_at accepts one), the others by 1-based index into each quest's stages array. The hub is 'hub'; topic nodes return to it; 'bye' ends. The 'wake' greeting is also what she says first when a new game hands over (core:opening/new_game's greeter).

greetings.text: There you are. Eyes working? Good. Don't look behind you yet. Come to the fire.
North. Walk the stones to the Choir, and keep your hands off the colossi.
Merrowby's talking. That's Merrowby's whole trade, but it's talking louder than usual.
Four lines on the Roll this year. I'd like it to stay four.
They're saying your name in Gullhithe now. Gullhithe. That's forty miles and a lake.
You've got that look people get when they've been kind somewhere and think nobody counted it. Somebody counted it.
Mullbourne's struck and clean. Pellam won't speak to me. That's mine to carry, not yours.
Late. I'm counting bells. Seventeen. Sixteen since spring, but I say seventeen and see if it argues.

greet.speaker: Wren Tallow
greet.text: Muddy boots, straight back, no idea where you are. You'll do.

choices.text: Who are you?
What is this place? What's the mist?
What am I supposed to call myself?
Where do we go from here?
Those things are waving at me.
The stone at the camp. What is it?
I'm ready for the cart.
The bell is humming. What does the village think?
I found a black stone tine in the Toll's crown.
Tell me about the Roll.
Harewell. Eleven households. Who were they?
Why send me to the Sayers and not go yourself?
What do you make of the Circle?
Tell me about the Wardens.
I have a name for the Roll. Mullbourne.
People are saying my name now.
Do you ever think about what I walked out of?
Harewell. You walked that down for two days.
I have been out to Harewell's lane. There is a lane.
Say that again about the hedge-wights.
Nothing. Carry on counting.

who_are_you.speaker: Wren Tallow
who_are_you.text: Wren Tallow. Warden of the Hearth, which sounds grander than it is. We keep a book of the names of villages, and we walk about making sure the villages are still under them. Mostly I chase bandits off the Larkbourne road and write down how many chickens a fox had. Twice in my life I've had to write a line in the Roll for a place that stopped being there. You are the third strange thing that has happened to me, and the other two were that.

the_hush.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_hush.text: That's the Hushline. South of here colour goes out of things, and sound, and then the things. Walk into it and the whisper turns you around, which is the kindest thing about it. Nobody comes out of it. I've stood at the top of that stair for nineteen years on and off and watched grey people walk down it, and I have never once watched anyone walk up.

choices.text: Until now.
What's on the other side?

the_hush_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_hush_2.text: Until now. Yes. I've been standing here for a while deciding whether to write you down, and in what book. Don't let that trouble you. It troubles me enough for both of us.

the_hush_3.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_hush_3.text: The songs say colour comes back further south. Songs say a lot. What's certainly on the other side is the Builders' city, the Choir, and a thing the Order sits up all night watching. You'd know better than me. You came from there.

the_naming_q.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_naming_q.text: You pick. That's not me being soft; that's how it works here. A name is not a label, it's a rope. Things that are named and spoken of stay put. Things nobody says go quiet, and then go. You came out of the quiet with nothing on you, so we tie the rope now, and we tie it in front of a witness, and I'm the witness. Say it clearly. I'll say it back and then it's done.

the_road.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_road.text: North. See the shoulders on the skyline, past the heath? That's the Sunken Choir: twelve of them, no heads, standing in a ring as if they were waiting to be let in. The road to Pilgrim's Ash starts past them. I've set stones along the way for the pilgrims, with a lamp on every third, so you can't miss it unless you mean to. Keep to them. Something with a bell on its back walks its round out on the heath, and it does not stop to ask names. You've my sword. If you want better, the pilgrims leave theirs at the Last Meal Stone, west of the Choir; nobody goes down into the Hush armed. Go on. I'll bring the cart round.

the_wights.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_wights.text: Greyfold's people. They sat down to wait out the Ash Winter a hundred and seventy years ago and they are still waiting and they still wave. They're slow, they're weak, and there are always more. Keep something in your legs. Swing when they stumble, not before. And don't feel clever about it afterwards; that's the part that goes wrong in people.

choices.text: They were farmers.
Understood.

the_wights_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_wights_2.text: They were. Every one. That's why we walk them down instead of burning the heath, and why the Order counts bells over them instead of saying prayers at them. Nobody's owed a prayer out here. Everyone's owed a count.

hearthstones.speaker: Wren Tallow
hearthstones.text: A Hearthstone. Put your hand flat on it and say your name aloud, so the stone has it too. Then if you die, and you will, you wake up at the last stone that heard you, with your teeth and your temper and nothing in your purse. Your marks stay where you fell, standing up in the shape of you until you fetch them. Die again on the way and the Echo goes quiet and your marks go with it. I've fetched mine three times. Two of them I had to fight past the thing that made me drop them, which is the joke.

the_cart.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_cart.text: Carter's going north with a load of pilgrims' bells for melting; grey folk leave them at the line and someone has to make spoons out of them eventually. I've bought your seat with Wardens' marks, which means you owe the Wardens and not me, which is deliberate. The Vale is warmer than this. That is not saying much, but it is saying something.

the_hum.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_hum.text: Forty metres of bronze in a hole in the ground and it's humming like a fly in a jug. Maud Brambling says it means a hard winter. Corwen Mullard says it means the Sayers have been at something. Old Pellam says he heard it once as a boy and won't say what happened after, which is the only answer I take seriously. Go and collect the village's opinions before the Wardens have one; once we have one, nobody says theirs.

choices.text: What do you think it means?
I'll ask around.

the_hum_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_hum_2.text: I think a bell that has been silent for a thousand and forty-three years does not start up for nothing, and I think you walked out of the south about a fortnight before it did. I'm not accusing you. I'm counting. Counting is what I do instead of worrying, and it is not working as well as usual.

the_tine.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_tine.text: Black stone, cold, sitting in a cradle up in the crown where nobody's climbed since Pellam's father. And it hums a half-note under the bell. Not with it. Under it, like two people singing who've stopped agreeing about the tune. The Builders made everything to hold a note. This one is holding the wrong one, or the bell is, and I don't know enough to say which and I'm not going to pretend otherwise in front of you.

choices.text: Could it be stopped?
Who would know?

the_tine_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_tine_2.text: You could wrap it in wool. I did. It hummed through the wool. I put it in the Roll room's iron box overnight and Pellam came down in the morning and asked who'd been singing.

the_tine_3.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_tine_3.text: The Sayers' Circle in Tollmere. They're mages, after a fashion: they hold that saying a thing loudly enough makes it more so. They'll know, and they'll charge, and they'll disagree with each other at length while they do it. That's not me being unkind. They're proud of it.

the_roll.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_roll.text: Every settlement in Hearthvale, in one book, in ink, since the Tending. When a place goes quiet, we don't cross it out; we write the line deeper and read it aloud on Tollday so that somebody living has said it that week. There are four lines like that now. Larkstead. Gosford. Mullbourne, which nobody has been able to find for a year. And Harewell, which is new since last Tollday.

choices.text: Does reading them aloud work?
Tell me about Harewell.
I see.

the_roll_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_roll_2.text: Pellam would say yes. Pellam has said those names at that bell every dawn for fifty years and there are still four of them, so you could equally say it hasn't. I'll tell you what I actually believe, and I'd thank you not to repeat it at the Rest: I think it works on us. I think a village that hears a dead village's name every week keeps its own doors painted.

harewell.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell.text: Harewell. On the down between here and Tamwick. Eleven households, a well with a hare cut on the lip, and a woman called Cille who sold hedge-honey at the Merrowby market on Tolldays. I bought honey from her. I cannot tell you what she looked like and I cannot find anyone who can, and last month I walked the down for two days and came back with nothing but a chalk doorstep worn hollow by feet, which is in the Roll room now in a box. You want to know what frightens a Warden? That. Not the barrows. That.

choices.text: How does a place just go?
What happens to people who lived there?

harewell_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_2.text: Quietly, and over about a generation, and everybody's busy. The road stops going there because the carter dies and the new carter has his own route. The Tollday stall isn't taken and nobody notices which one. Then one year the hedge grows across the lane and there's no lane. Nobody does it on purpose. That's what I hate about it. There's nobody to arrest.

harewell_3.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_3.text: That's the part the books skip. Some of them are elsewhere and have been for years and answer to other place-names now. Some of them are in the barrows, working. And some of them, I think, are simply not, in the way that a word you have forgotten is not. I put that question to a Sayer once. He talked for an hour. I came away knowing less, but more elegantly.

why_me.speaker: Wren Tallow
why_me.text: Three reasons, and you get all three because you'd work them out. One: the Circle charges Wardens double and always has, over a matter from before I was born involving a bridge. Two: a letter is cheaper than a Warden and I'm needed on the Larkbourne road, where the Boys are back. Three, and this is the real one: they'll want to look at you. Somebody walked up the Hushline Stair and a fortnight later the Toll started humming. If I take them the tine, they'll put it in a drawer. If you take them the tine, they'll put you in a chair and talk for three days, and somewhere in the third day one of them will say something true by accident.

the_circle.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_circle.text: Three lectures and three answers and every one of them delivered like it's the only one in the building. Don't let it sour you. The Circle is honest in an odd way: they teach all three accounts and forbid you to prefer one out loud, which is more than the Order does and considerably more than I do. Sulion will be right about the bell. Cresswell will be right about the village. Ondrael will be right about the deep places, and she'll look ill while she says it.

choices.text: Which do you believe?
Noted.

the_circle_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_circle_2.text: The Candle, on weekdays. A village that talks stays warm; I've watched it be true for nineteen years. On Tollday, when I'm at the Rest reading four names aloud to an empty room, I believe the Breath, and I go home early.

the_wardens.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_wardens.text: Eighty-odd of us across the Vale, a fort at the Rest that's really a waystation with opinions, and one book. We're the law here, which mostly means fines, a cell with a window, and telling two farmers which of them owns a ditch. The Roll is the real work. Everything else is what we do between Tolldays so that we're fit enough to walk to the places on it.

choices.text: Could I join?
Who else keeps the Roll?

the_wardens_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_wardens_2.text: Ask me again when you've done something in this valley that somebody else will describe to a third person. That's not a riddle, it's the actual requirement. A Warden who isn't talked about can't do the job; nobody opens a door to a stranger with a book.

the_wardens_3.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_wardens_3.text: Pellam Ashcombe kept it for forty years and his hands have gone, so I copy for him and he corrects me, which he enjoys enormously. He's up at the crater rim every dawn saying the quiet names to the bell. If you want to understand this valley faster than I can explain it, go and stand next to him at first light and don't talk.

mullbourne.speaker: Wren Tallow
mullbourne.text: Mullbourne. Say it again. — Mullbourne. Nine households, soft ground, a mill that never worked. That's a year of my life you've just handed back to me in three syllables. Now the hard half. Custom says a found name with nobody living to tend it gets written in fresh ink, read aloud once by a Warden, and struck through, so that it is kept and finished and nobody spends another year walking a down for it. Pellam says a struck name is a place that never was. Pellam is eighty-one and says the names at dawn because the alternative is not saying them.

choices.text: Then don't strike it. Let Pellam have it.
Strike it. Let the walking stop.
I haven't decided.

mullbourne_keep.speaker: Wren Tallow
mullbourne_keep.text: Then it stays open and I keep walking, and one of these years I'll find a doorstep. Fine. Tell him yourself; he'd rather hear it from you, and he'll make you say it twice.

mullbourne_strike.speaker: Wren Tallow
mullbourne_strike.text: Fresh ink, read once, line through. I'll do it on Tollday with the door open so it's witnessed. And I'll be the one who tells Pellam, not you; that's a Warden's job and I'd like to keep one or two of them. He won't speak to me for a season. He'll still correct my copying. That's Pellam.

on_renown.speaker: Wren Tallow
on_renown.text: They are. Bessa Tamwick had a version of you at market that was eight feet tall and Bennick Cresswell has a worse one going round Tollmere. Good. I mean that plainly: it's good. You're a person who came out of the quiet with no rope on them, and every mouth that says your name is another hand on it. Enjoy it, don't believe it, and remember that the ones who spread it can stop.

choices.text: Does it go the other way too?
I'll try to stay unimpressed with myself.

on_renown_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
on_renown_2.text: You've seen a Hollow village, have you? Doors barred at noon, dogs sent in, children counted twice. A name can be a rope or a rope can be a thing round a neck, and the valley decides which, not you. I've never seen anyone talk their way out of what they did in front of witnesses. I have seen people outlive it. Takes about a decade and a lot of carrying things for other people.

the_foundling.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_foundling.text: Every night, since you ask, which I wish you hadn't. Here's where I've got to. Either you are someone who was so thoroughly unsaid that there was nothing left to hold you there, and you drifted out the way a boat comes off a slipway. Or something in the south let go of you on purpose and I walked it up the stair by the hand and gave it a name and a cart fare. I've decided to act as though it's the first. If I'm wrong, I'd rather be wrong having been decent about it.

choices.text: That's a lot of trust.
It might be the second.

the_foundling_2.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_foundling_2.text: It's not trust, it's method. Wardens name things. It's the only tool in the bag. When a thing comes out of the dark, you say what it is as loudly and specifically as you can, in front of other people, and then you all know where you stand with it. That's all I did to you. Don't make me regret the method; I haven't got another.

the_foundling_3.speaker: Wren Tallow
the_foundling_3.text: Then it made one mistake, which was letting go of you in front of a woman with a book. You're written down now. Whatever you were before, there are eleven people in Merrowby who would notice if you stopped coming to market, and that is not nothing. That is, as far as anyone in this valley can tell, the only thing that has ever worked.

harewell_offer.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_offer.text: Two days, and a chalk doorstep in a box, and eleven people I cannot describe. — I'll tell you the part I've not written. I went out there twice more. Both times I walked the down from the shrine to the scarp and came back and could not have told you whether there was a lane in it. Not 'there was no lane'. Could not have told you. That is not a thing that happens to me; I count for a living. So I stopped going, which I am not proud of, and I have been waiting for somebody who never bought honey off Cille to go and look at the same ground with eyes that have nothing in them.

choices.text: I'll walk it. What am I looking for?
You want a witness, not a Warden.
Not today.

harewell_witness.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_witness.text: I want both and I'll take either. — A Warden goes and writes down what is there. A witness goes and is somebody the thing happened in front of. I have been the first one out there three times and got nothing, and it has occurred to me lately, at about four in the morning, that a place which goes quiet when nobody says its name might also go quiet in the eye of somebody who has been saying it wrong for a year. I have been saying Harewell every Tollday since it went on. Perhaps I have worn it smooth.

choices.text: Then I'll go. What am I looking for?
I'll think about it.

harewell_accept.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_accept.text: The doorstep first. It's in the Roll room at the Rest, on the shelf under the window, in a box, and Hesk will want it back and will say so twice. Carry it out to the hedge shrine — Ansel's, the hawthorn grown through the stone chair — and then walk east along the hedge line until the ground goes flat in a square, and stand the doorstep where you think the lane was. — And mind what's working those hedges. I've seen it. It has a billhook and it doesn't stop for a greeting, and I want it written down that I told you and not that you found out.

harewell_line.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_line.text: There is a lane. Say it again where I can write it. — Right. Then here is the Roll room's question and I'd rather have your answer than mine, because mine has been the same for a year and has got us a box on a shelf. What does the line say? That a Warden walked the ground and found it, with the doorstep stood up where the lane runs, for anybody who comes after to trip over. Or that the doorstep is evidence and goes back in the box, and the line stays as it is, which is honest and which is a shelf. Or you take it to Tamwick, where some steward wrote 'ask Tamwick' in a margin thirteen years ago and never did, and make Tamwick keep it.

choices.text: Stand it in the lane. A Warden walked the ground and found it.
Back in the box. It is evidence, not a grave marker.
Tamwick keeps it. Somebody there owes that margin an answer.
Give me a day on it.

harewell_written.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_written.text: Written, and read back, and I'll read it out on Tollday with the door open. — Walk with me as far as the ford. I have got something the wrong way round for a year and I would like to say it out loud to somebody who will not be kind about it.

harewell_after.speaker: Wren Tallow
harewell_after.text: A hedge-wight is a farmer who did not stop. That is not folklore, that is the Rest's own bestiary page and I have written it out for recruits. — Harewell had eleven households. I have now met four of them, out on that down, working a hedge that has no field behind it, with their own tools. I put two of them down myself in 1039 and wrote 'wights, two' in the day-book and went home and had my supper. — I am not going to make a speech. I would like it noted that I did not see it, that you did, and that the difference between us is that you had never bought honey off any of them.

bye.speaker: Wren Tallow
bye.text: Go on. Mind the road past the mill; the Boys are back and they're getting brave about it.
